comments.text:
Before comparing Haiti to its neighbor, or suggesting the transatlantic slave trade had any upside, here's what the historical record actually documents, with sources.
On dehumanization. Under the Code Noir, an enslaved person had no legal status as a human being — they were classified as movable property, sellable, separable from their children, subject to mutilation as punishment without that constituting a crime. Saint-Domingue was the most profitable colony in the world precisely because the average life expectancy of an enslaved person on the sugar plantations was barely seven years — the economic logic favored replacement over upkeep. It was against this backdrop that in 1791, the enslaved population of Saint-Domingue rose up, and in 1804 defeated Napoleon Bonaparte's army to found the first nation to abolish slavery in its constitution.
On the 1825 debt. On April 17, 1825, under threat from 14 French warships poised to bombard Port-au-Prince, France imposed on Haiti an indemnity of 150 million gold francs — 16 times Haiti's 1826 GDP  (Amnesty International) — in exchange for recognizing an independence Haiti had already won militarily twenty years earlier. Haiti kept repaying this sum, borrowed at usurious rates from French banks, until 1952. A 2021 academic study calculated the resulting loss: without that indemnity, Haiti's per-capita income in 2018 could have been nearly six times higher — comparable to that of neighboring Dominican Republic.  (France 24)
On the American occupation. On December 17, 1914, U.S. Marines seized $500,000 in gold reserves from Haiti's National Bank, transferred directly to New York's National City Bank, with the Haitian government's protests achieving nothing.  (Haiti Liberte) That seizure preceded a 19-year military occupation (1915–1934), during which Haiti's constitution was rewritten under duress to permit foreign land ownership, and forced labor was reintroduced through the corvée system: peasants were seized off rural roads, pulled from their farms, held in camps overnight, and abused  (Haitisolidarity) to build infrastructure that served American companies, not Haiti.
The development gap between Haiti and its neighbor is not the product of some cultural or national deficiency. It's the measurable result of two centuries of successive financial extraction and military control, first by France, then by the United States — documented in state archives, confirmed by academic research, and now acknowledged by the UN and debated in the French parliament. Framing the transatlantic slave trade as "a good thing" ignores both what the system actually was and its calculated, two-century cost.
